before:
A model contains learned numerical settings called weights. Some services let us send requests but do not let us obtain those weights. Other models publish weights that can be downloaded. Having the files makes some additional checks possible, but it does not automatically tell us why every answer was produced or where every training example came from.

It therefore helps to separate the questions before choosing the tools. Reconstructing a payment, checking whether a model reacts correctly to a changed fact, and inspecting its internal calculations are different jobs. Each needs its own evidence and its own test.

The expense policy below is intentionally simple enough for a conventional rules program to solve. That gives us a known answer for every claim and keeps the focus on what can be checked. We compare what a reviewer can establish from saved interactions with hosted assistants and what extra inspection becomes possible with a small model running locally.
after:
Holding the weight files makes some extra checks possible: running the model again on your own machine, reading the numbers it computes along the way, or changing one weight and watching the answer move. The files do not by themselves say why every answer was produced or where the training examples came from.

A team choosing an assistant for decisions like these has to decide what it will need to show an auditor later, and whether that requires holding the model's files. A closed hosted model may be the most capable option on offer; an open-weight model can be inspected but may make more mistakes. The choice should follow from the audit questions the team must answer. Reconstructing a payment, checking that the assistant reacts correctly when one fact changes, and inspecting the model's internal calculations are different jobs, and each needs its own evidence. This study tries each of those checks on a task whose right answers are known exactly.

before:
Preparing a presentation means shaping ideas and numbers into something an audience can follow. In a project review, the slides might compare a few options and explain the figures behind a recommendation. When the plan changes, keeping those figures and the timeline consistent helps the discussion stay clear.

A model has to decide what to emphasize, choose a useful chart or diagram, and fit the content into a readable layout. A written slide description cannot fully show how PowerPoint will wrap a title or crowd its labels. Even correct risk values can tell the wrong story if they sit at the wrong coordinates on a matrix.
after:
A careful person lists every slide where a changed number appears, recalculates each one, and then looks at the finished slides, because a longer title can wrap into the text below it and a risk can land in the wrong square even when its label is right. The mistakes that get through are quiet ones: an old payback left on the closing slide, or R5 drawn one square too low. A committee can approve or reject a plan because of either.

A language model can write the words for a slide, but it cannot see the slide. In this study each model describes every slide in a structured text format: a text box with this wording at this position and size, a table with these cells here, a bar chart with these values there. A program turns that description into an editable PowerPoint file. The model chooses coordinates and font sizes, but it never sees where PowerPoint breaks a line, so it cannot tell whether a title fits until the slide is drawn.

before: An **audit** is a check against a stated requirement using evidence. Here, **closed model** means a hosted model whose weights are unavailable to us. **Open-weight model** means that published weights can be obtained under their licence. The Open Source Initiative's [definition](https://opensource.org/ai/open-source-ai-definition) also requires training and inference code and sufficiently detailed training-data information. after: A language model is a large set of learned numbers called **weights**, plus the code that runs them. Some models are offered only as a service: you send text, you get text back, and the weights stay on the provider's computers. This study calls these closed models. Other models publish their weights so that anyone can download and run them; these are open-weight models. "Open source" asks for more. The Open Source Initiative's [definition of open-source AI](https://opensource.org/ai/open-source-ai-definition) also requires the training and inference code and detailed information about the training data, so downloadable weights alone do not meet it.
